# Where is the sun, relative to the camera?

## Short answer

The sun is **behind the camera and off to the camera's left**, and it is **well up
in the sky — roughly 40° above the horizon**, not near the horizon. In plain terms
the camera is shooting *with the sun over its left shoulder*: the sun sits about
25–30° round to the left of "directly behind the lens", so it is very nearly
back-lighting the camera operator and front-lighting everything the lens is
pointed at.

Because of that, **every cast shadow in the picture runs away from the camera and
toward the right of frame** — forward in the direction of travel, leaning about
25–30° to the right of the street's centreline, and spilling from the left-hand
side of the street toward the right-hand side. Nothing casts a shadow back toward
the lens.

**This does not change during the video.** The sun stays in essentially the same
place relative to the camera from the first frame to the last, because the camera
is bolted to the front of a streetcar that runs in a straight line in one fixed
compass direction for the whole take. There is no moment where the lighting flips
from front-lit to back-lit, no moment where shadows swing across to the other
side, and the 50-second running time is far too short for the sun itself to move
appreciably (it moves about 12 arc-minutes of azimuth in 50 seconds).

## What the footage is, and why the camera's heading matters

The camera looks forward from the front of a streetcar travelling down Market
Street, San Francisco — the title card reads "San Francisco, Market Street, April
1906" (this is the well-known "A Trip Down Market Street" film). The live footage
runs from about 0:01 to about 0:43; the last seven seconds are black.

The Ferry Building and its clock tower are dead ahead in the distance from the
start and grow steadily larger until the streetcar arrives at the terminal, so the
camera's viewing direction is locked at roughly **north-east (about 40°)** for the
entire ride. That fixed heading is exactly why the sun's position relative to the
camera is constant. Looking north-east means the camera's left-hand side faces
north-west and its right-hand side faces south-east.

## The evidence, point by point

**1. Surfaces that face the camera are in direct sun — so the sun is behind the
camera.** The Ferry Building's big arcaded facade at the foot of Market Street
faces straight back down the street, i.e. straight into the lens. From about 0:33
onward that facade is unmistakably in direct sunlight: the pilasters and arch
faces read bright white while the arch soffits and recesses are crisply dark. A
wall that faces the camera can only be in direct sun if the sun is on the camera's
side of it. The same holds for the crowd on the plaza in front of it, who are lit
on the sides turned toward the lens.

**2. There is no back-lighting anywhere.** If the sun were ahead of the camera the
footage would be contre-jour — silhouetted people and vehicles, veiling flare, and
shadows pointing down-frame toward the lens. Instead the scene is consistently
front-lit, with detail on the near faces of everything ahead, and every shadow I
could trace points away from the camera.

**3. Shadows measurably run forward-and-right.** I calibrated the ground plane
from the tram rails (standard 1.435 m gauge): the rails give a forward vanishing
point at about x = 261, a horizon at about y = 167, and a camera height of about
2.2 m above the roadway. With that calibration, two shadows measured on clean
sunlit pavement give:

- The man walking away from the camera on the Ferry Building plaza at about 0:41:
  his shadow leaves his feet and runs **sideways to the right by about 0.73 m**
  while receding slightly from the camera. For a man of about 1.65 m that implies
  a sun azimuth of about 244° and an elevation of about 44°.
- The wagon in mid-street at about 0:36: its shadow extends **to the right by about
  1.2 m** of lateral offset, again receding slightly. That implies a sun azimuth of
  about 248° and an elevation of about 40°.

Both objects put the shadow tip *higher* in the frame than the shadow base, which
means the shadows genuinely recede into the distance — they point away from the
camera, not toward it. Two independent measurements agreeing is the main reason I
am confident about the left-rear placement rather than a pure side-light.

**4. The sunlit and shaded sides of the street are the ones a left-rear sun
requires.** Averaged over the whole ride, the building fronts on the **right** of
frame are consistently brighter than those on the **left** — ratios of 1.24 to
1.57 in matched bands of rows, measured separately over 0:04–0:10, 0:10–0:20,
0:20–0:30 and 0:30–0:43. The right-hand fronts (facing north-west) look back
toward the sun and are washed in direct light; the left-hand fronts (facing
south-east) face away from it and sit in their own shade. The fact that the ratio
is greater than 1 in *every* segment is direct evidence that the sun never changes
sides during the video. Correspondingly, in the wider shots the left-hand building
row throws its shadow rightwards onto part of the roadway while the rest of the
carriageway is in full sun.

**5. The camera's own streetcar throws its shadow forward and to the right.** A
temporal median of the straight run averages away all the moving traffic and
leaves a persistent grey wedge lying on the roadway on the **right** of the
tracks — fixed in the frame while the world streams past it, which is the
signature of something attached to the camera. Converted to ground coordinates it
sits about 2.6–3.5 m to the right of the track centreline. For a streetcar about
2.4 m wide and about 3.3 m to the roof, a sun at azimuth 245° and elevation 42°
predicts its roof shadow landing about 2.9 m right of centre — a match. So the
vehicle carrying the camera is casting its own shadow ahead and to its right,
which is only possible with the sun behind it and to its left.

**6. The sun is fairly high, not a low raking sun.** All the shadows are short:
the man's shadow is a little under half his height in lateral extent, and the
wagons' shadows are compact pools beside and beneath them rather than long
streaks. A low sun would also have thrown the whole multi-storey building row on
the left clear across the wide roadway, which plainly does not happen. The
measured shadow-length-to-height ratios put the sun at about **40–45° elevation**.

## Putting numbers on it

- Camera heading: about 40° (north-east), constant.
- Sun azimuth: about **245°** (west-south-west), i.e. about 205° clockwise from
  where the lens points, which is the same as **about 155° round to the left** —
  so roughly 25–30° off from being exactly behind the camera, displaced toward the
  camera's left.
- Sun elevation: about **40–45°** above the horizon.
- Resulting shadow direction: azimuth about 65°, i.e. pointing away from the
  camera and about 25–30° to the right of the direction of travel.
- For mid-April in San Francisco that solar position corresponds to roughly
  **3 p.m. local standard time** — a mid-afternoon sun, well past the meridian.

I'd treat the compass figures as good to maybe ±10° in azimuth and ±5° in
elevation: the footage is soft, heavily motion-blurred and low-contrast, the
shadow tips fade out rather than ending sharply, and the pedestrian's and wagon's
true heights had to be assumed.

## Summary

Throughout the entire video the sun is behind the camera and to its left, about
40–45° up — over the camera's left shoulder, roughly west-south-west while the
camera looks north-east. The scene is therefore front-lit, and all shadows fall
away from the lens and toward the right of frame. This geometry is the same in the
first second and the last, because the camera's heading never changes during the
ride.

The video is the 1906 film shot from the front of a cable car travelling along Market Street, San Francisco, toward the Ferry Building at the far end of the street (the title card reads "San Francisco, Market Street, April, 1906"). The camera points straight ahead down the street for the whole trip. At about 43 seconds the car slows and stops in front of a stone pier of the Ferry Building (a plinth with an inscription fills the frame) and the picture fades to white, then black. There is no real change of heading, so the camera faces the same direction from the first frame to the last.

## Evidence from the shadows

1. Horse-drawn delivery wagon directly ahead on the tracks (about 33 to 36 seconds). This is the clearest shadow in the film. The wagon's shadow is a dark patch on the roadway on the RIGHT-hand side of the wagon, poking out beyond its right-hand wheels, and it lies level with or slightly beyond the wheels in depth, i.e. away from the camera. The patch moves with the wagon frame after frame, so it is a shadow and not a mark on the road. The ground between the camera and the wagon (lower left of the wagon, between the rails) is fully sunlit with no shadow at all. So the wagon's shadow falls forward and to the right, which means the light comes from behind the camera and from its left.

2. Cable car on the left-hand track at about 16 seconds. Its shadow lies on the road to the right of the car, spreading toward the centre of the street. Again the shadow is on the right side of the object.

3. Automobile beside the tracks at about 24 seconds, and the covered wagon at about 8 seconds. Both show their dark ground shadow at their base extending to the right, with bright, shadow-free ground on the camera side.

4. Pedestrians standing in the roadway (the man beside the tracks at about 24 seconds, the men in front of the Ferry Building at about 40 to 42 seconds) cast no shadow back toward the camera; the pavement between them and the camera is bright. Their shadows lie beside and ahead of them, hidden behind or to the right of their bodies.

5. Building lighting. The facades on the right-hand side of the street are bright and sunlit (awnings and window details are clearly lit), while the facades and sidewalk on the left-hand side of the street are in shade, with a dark band of building shadow running along the left edge of the roadway. The Ferry Building facade, which faces the camera at the end of the street, is brightly lit almost face-on, and the inscribed plinth in the final frames is in full sun. Surfaces facing the camera and surfaces on the right can only be sunlit if the light comes from behind the camera and from its left.

6. There is no backlighting, no lens flare, and no silhouetting of people or vehicles against a bright sky, which rules out the sun being in front of the camera.

## Conclusion

- Direction: the sun is BEHIND the camera and to the LEFT, roughly in the rear-left quarter, closer to directly behind than to directly left (the forward component of the shadows is larger than the sideways component, which is only about half an object's width).
- Height: the visible shadows are moderate in length, on the order of one object height, so the sun is fairly high, roughly 35 to 45 degrees above the horizon, not low on the horizon and not overhead.
- Over time: this relationship is the same throughout the video. The cable car runs in a straight line along one street and the camera never changes heading, so the sun stays behind-left of the camera from the start until the picture fades out at the Ferry Building.

Geographically this makes sense. Market Street runs from south-west to north-east and the camera is looking north-east toward the Ferry Building, so a sun behind and to the left of the camera is a sun in the south-west to west, i.e. a mid-to-late afternoon sun, with the shadows pointing north-east to east, up the street and slightly toward its south-eastern side.
